title: Preface
summary: A 1962 President's Office File (Box 115) on the Cuban Missile Crisis, covering Khrushchev-Kennedy correspondence from 10/23/62 to 12/19/62. It includes official translations and Russian originals of Khrushchev letters (10/23, 10/24, 10/26), Gromyko and Smirnovski covering notes, State Department and White House memos (Brubeck to Bundy, Kennedy memo on Dobrynin meeting), and several undated or unsigned letters. Khrushchev's 10/23 letter protests the US quarantine and inspection of ships to Cuba and calls for US restraint.

title: rocno,nHH IlpesH,neHT,
summary: A Soviet government letter replying to the U.S. President's October 22 statement on Cuba. It rejects the U.S. naval blockade and ship inspections as violations of the UN Charter and freedom of the seas, and as aggressive acts against Cuba and the USSR. It states that Cuba's defensive weapons serve only its self-defense, that the U.S. bears responsibility for catastrophic consequences, and that the USSR will not accept U.S. control over Soviet ships.

title: EYES ONLY
summary: OCR'd Khrushchev letter to Kennedy (Oct 26, 1962, Moscow, Section One of Four), with Kennedy's inserted notes. Khrushchev says the US and USSR have publicly exchanged views on Cuba and that secret letters can't help; he denies offensive weapons in Cuba, saying the arms are defensive and sent at Cuba's request. He argues war is a calamity, warns that attacking Cuba would bring retaliation, and calls the US fears irrational. Includes margin notes (relayed to the White House, 9:35 PM) and a 'Verbatim Text' header.

nodes.title: -2- 1101, OCTOBER 26, 7 PM {SECTION TW? OF FOUR) FROM MOSCOW (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt of a 1962 Soviet message (October 26, section two of four, from Moscow) to the US President during the Cuban Missile Crisis. It states the USSR wants peace and coexistence, insists ideological and economic disputes be settled by peaceful competition rather than military means, denounces the US naval 'quarantine' around Cuba as piracy, claims Soviet ships carry only peaceful cargo with no weapons, and admits earlier weapons shipments that Cuba already received for defense. It urges restraint and control of passions.

nodes.title: -3- 1101, OCTOBER 26, 7 PM (SECTION TWO OF FOUR) FR0f1 MOSCOW
nodes.summary: Excerpts of the October 26, 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis exchange between Khrushchev's Moscow government and the US. Moscow argues that stopping Soviet ships would be piracy and that defensive measures would follow. It accepts a UN Acting Secretary-General proposal to pause arms shipments to Cuba while negotiations proceed, and says the US must not attack vessels. It defends Soviet aid to Cuba as humanitarian and cites US intervention in Siberia and the threat of invasion. It proposes trading the Soviet missiles for a US pledge not to invade Cuba, and it notes the White House relay times.

nodes.title: POLICY
POLICY (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpts from the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis record: Khrushchev's October 26, 1962 letter to Kennedy warning that US aggressive actions in international waters risk nuclear war and proposing to untie the 'knot' if the US pledges no invasion of Cuba; and Attorney General Robert Kennedy's October 30, 1962 memo on his meeting with Ambassador Dobrynin, reporting a U-2 shot down over Cuba, demanding removal of Soviet missile bases within a day, and rejecting any quid pro quo on Turkey. Also includes a November 3, 1962 State Department transmittal of the letter's translation.

nodes.title: A. rpoMhIKo
nodes.summary: The text is a Russian-language 1962 letter from Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev to U.S. President John F. Kennedy, transmitted via Foreign Minister A. Gromyko during the Cuban Missile Crisis. Khrushchev says both sides have voiced their views on the crisis and that the conflict risks war. He argues that the Soviet Union is not seeking war and that the dispute is a serious threat. He calls the U.S. naval quarantine of Cuba an act of aggression and says Soviet ships carry no weapons. He proposes that the USSR would withdraw missiles from Cuba if the U.S. pledges not to invade Cuba, framing it as a mutual compromise for world peace.

POLICY section excerpts from the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis record. Includes Khrushchev's October 26, 1962 letter warning that US actions in international waters risk nuclear war and proposing removal of Soviet missiles from Cuba if the US pledges no invasion; Attorney General Robert Kennedy's October 30, 1962 memo on meeting Ambassador Dobrynin (U-2 shot down over Cuba, demand to remove Soviet missile bases within a day, no quid pro quo on Turkey); and a November 3, 1962 State Department transmittal of the letter's translation. Also a Russian-language letter from Khrushchev via Gromyko calling the US naval quarantine aggression and stating Soviet ships carry no weapons.

summary: Excerpts from the October 26, 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis exchanges between Khrushchev's Soviet government and the US. Moscow calls the US naval quarantine of Cuba piracy, says Soviet ships carry only peaceful cargo, and urges restraint. It accepts a UN proposal to pause arms shipments, defends aid to Cuba, and proposes trading Soviet missiles for a US pledge not to invade Cuba. Also covers Robert Kennedy's October 30 memo on meeting Dobrynin (U-2 shootdown, demand to remove missile bases, no Turkey quid pro quo) and a November 3 State Department translation transmittal.

title: DEPARTMENT OF STATE
summary: A 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis correspondence between Soviet Premier Khrushchev and U.S. President Kennedy. Khrushchev rejects U.S. claims that Soviet weapons in Cuba are offensive, condemns the U.S. naval 'quarantine' as piracy, and argues for peaceful coexistence. He proposes mutual non-shipment of arms and non-invasion of Cuba, cites U.S. aggression in Siberia, and references U Thant's proposals. Later letters record the agreement: Soviet missile removal in exchange for lifting the quarantine and a non-invasion pledge, plus disputes over IL-28 bombers, UN verification, observation posts, overflights, and formal documentation. Khrushchev also addresses nuclear test ban talks, seismic stations, the German peace treaty, West Berlin, and Cuban conditions.

title: EYES~
summary: Khrushchev's December 1962 letter to Kennedy proposes accepting 2-3 on-site inspections yearly in seismic areas of nuclear powers, using national detection plus automatic seismic stations, with anti-espionage safeguards like Soviet-piloted planes and no cameras, to reach a nuclear test ban starting January 1, 1963. It cites the Cuban crisis resolution and UN calls, and urges ending nuclear explosions as a step toward disarmament. Also included: JFK Library archivist notes that only pages 1 and 8 survive, and a Russian-language Khrushchev letter of October 28, 1962, on Cuba, the Soviet aid pledge, and an envoy to New York.
